n: Joseph Smith had been imprisoned for months in the cold, cramped lower room of Liberty Jail while the Saints were driven from Missouri. In a letter dated March 20, 1839, he cries out like the psalmists: where is God? Why is he hidden?

f.g: A tent or canopy; here, the covering that seems to hide God from view.

n: How long will God hold back while he sees and hears his people’s suffering? Joseph’s honesty with God models real prayer in anguish.

f.g: Held back, restrained.

n: Joseph asks how long the injustices will go on before God’s heart is moved. “Bowels” in old English meant the inner seat of tender feelings.

f.g: Bowels = innermost feelings; compassion felt deep inside.

n: Joseph reminds God—and himself—that God created everything and controls even the devil and hell. Then comes a rush of pleas: reach out, see, hear, uncover, soften.

f.g: Hebrew for the realm of the dead; the underworld.
Overtaken by darkness.

n: Joseph asks God to defend his people against their enemies—an honest, raw cry for justice, like the imprecatory psalms.
He closes his plea simply: remember your suffering Saints, and we will praise you forever.
The Lord answers tenderly, calling Joseph “my son.” Compared to eternity, his trials will be brief. These words have comforted countless people in hard times.

f.w: My son, peace be unto thy soul

n: The key is not just enduring, but enduring well—with faith and without bitterness. Then God will lift him up.
Joseph is reminded that many friends still stand by him and will welcome him warmly again.

f.w: Thy friends do stand by thee
f.g: Saints such as Emma Smith, Brigham Young, and others continued to support him and visited or wrote to him in jail.

n: Joseph is not as badly off as Job, whose friends accused him of secret sin. Perspective can ease suffering.

f.w: Thou art not yet as Job

n: Those falsely accusing Joseph will see their hopes vanish like frost melting under the morning sun.

f.g: White frost formed on cold mornings.

n: God has determined to change circumstances and will let schemers be caught in their own cleverness.

f.w: take them in their own craftiness

f.g: Formally decreed, as with a signature and wax seal.

n: What they wish on others will come back on themselves—a common biblical principle of justice.
Their plans against the Saints will be disappointed.

f.w: their hopes may be cut off

n: A strong prophetic warning that persecutors and their families would not endure. “To stand by the wall” is a biblical idiom for surviving descendants.

f.w: not one of them is left to stand by the wall
f.g: An idiom from Old Testament curses meaning no one survives.

n: Cursed are those who “lift up the heel”—turn against—the Lord’s anointed, accusing them of sin when they have done what God commanded.

f.g: To kick or turn against, especially in betrayal.
Right, proper.

n: Those who loudly accuse God’s servants of sin often act from their own sin and rebellion.
Some had sworn false testimony to put Church leaders in prison or get them killed. Several former members testified against Joseph in Missouri.
They have harmed the Lord’s “little ones”—his humble followers—and will be cut off from temple blessings.
Their prosperity will fail, and even those who once flattered them will despise them.

f.w: Their basket shall not be full

n: They forfeit the right to the priesthood for themselves and their descendants who follow them in that course.

f.w: They shall not have right to the priesthood
f.g: Priesthood is held by righteousness; persistent opposition to God’s work forfeits it.

n: Echoing Jesus’ words, it would be better for them to drown with a millstone around their necks.

f.w: a millstone had been hanged about their necks

f.g: A heavy round stone for grinding grain.

n: Woe to those who trouble, drive, murder, and testify against God’s people. Jesus called the hypocrites of his day “a generation of vipers.”

f.g: Distress, trouble.

n: God sees all their deeds and has a swift judgment held in reserve at the right time.

f.g: At its proper, appointed time.

n: Every person has an appointed time to answer for their works.

f.w: a time appointed for every man

n: The tone turns hopeful. God will reveal knowledge by the Holy Ghost that has never been revealed before—a promise Joseph saw fulfilled in Nauvoo.

f.w: the unspeakable gift of the Holy Ghost

n: Ancient prophets looked forward eagerly to this day; angels pointed them to it as reserved for the completion of their glory.
In this coming time nothing will be withheld—including truths about God and other divine beings.

f.w: whether there be one God or many gods

n: Heavenly thrones and powers will be revealed to—and bestowed on—those who stay valiant in the gospel of Jesus Christ.

f.w: thrones and dominions, principalities and powers

n: Even the limits of the heavens, seas, land, sun, moon, and stars will be revealed.

f.g: The boundaries, laws, and limits of the universe.

n: All the cycles, times, laws, and glories of the heavenly bodies will be revealed in the dispensation of the fulness of times.

f.g: Orbits or rotations of heavenly bodies.

f.w: dispensation of the fulness of times

n: This was planned in a council of the eternal God before the world was created—to be revealed at the end, when everyone enters God’s presence and rest.
Joseph gives a vivid image: trying to stop God from pouring knowledge on the Saints is like trying to stop the Missouri River with your arm. Running water cleans itself; truth will prevail.

f.w: How long can rolling waters remain impure?
f.g: Moving water purifies itself over time—an image of truth overcoming error.
Small and weak.

n: A famous question: many are called to serve, but few are chosen. Why?

f.w: many called, but few are chosen

n: Because their hearts are set on worldly things and on people’s praise, they miss the essential lesson that follows.

f.w: aspire to the honors of men

n: The lesson: priesthood rights are bound to heaven’s powers, and those powers work only through righteousness. Authority without goodness is empty.

f.g: The actual power of God that makes priesthood effective, distinct from the office itself.

n: Priesthood can be conferred, but when someone uses it to hide sin, feed pride, or control others unrighteously “in any degree,” heaven withdraws. “Amen to the priesthood” means it is finished for that man.

f.g: That is, the end of it; his priesthood power ceases.
Force or pressure that overrides another’s will.

n: Before he knows it, such a person is left alone, fighting God like an ox kicking against the goad.

f.g: Pricks = sharp goads used to drive oxen; kicking them only hurts the ox.
Before.

n: A frank warning learned through hard experience: almost everyone who gets a little authority is tempted to misuse it.

f.g: Using position or power to control, manipulate, or force others.

n: That is why many are called but few are chosen.

f.g: For this reason.

n: True influence comes not from position but from persuasion, patience, gentleness, meekness, and sincere love. This applies to parents, leaders, and spouses as much as priesthood holders.

f.g: Genuine, sincere love; not faked.
Convincing by reason and love rather than force.

n: Add kindness and true knowledge, which expand the soul—without hypocrisy or deceit.

f.g: Without deceit or trickery.

n: Sometimes correction is needed—“betimes” means promptly or at the right time, and only when prompted by the Holy Ghost. Afterward, show more love so the person knows you are not an enemy.

f.g: Early, promptly; at the appropriate moment (not “sometimes”).
Clarity and directness, not harshness or anger.

n: So he will know your loyalty is stronger than death itself.
Be full of charity toward everyone and let virtue adorn your thoughts constantly. Then confidence before God grows, and priesthood understanding settles on the soul gently, like dew.

f.w: let virtue garnish thy thoughts unceasingly
f.g: Garnish = decorate, adorn.

f.w: distil upon thy soul as the dews from heaven

n: The promised result: the Holy Ghost as a constant companion, a scepter of righteousness, and an everlasting dominion that comes freely, without force—because it rests on love.

f.g: A ruler’s staff, symbol of authority.
